LOGIC ADVENTURES

Thirty picture puzzles you really play.

Patterns, odd-one-outs, shadow matches, size orders, mazes, secret codes and clue hunts — real logic puzzles played right on our own puzzle artwork, with plain text instructions a grown-up can read aloud.

Every card is one real game. 30 of the planned 30 adventures are playable now — 01, 18 and 25 join the moment their artwork is uploaded. Progress is saved on this device for the child chosen in My Classroom.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What each game practises.

The collection climbs one slope: finishing patterns (Robot’s rainbow, Turtle’s bridges, Octopus’s shells, Dragon’s crystals), catching odd ones (Dinosaur eggs, Monkey’s market, Hedgehog’s garden), matching shadows and sizes (Lion’s safari, Elephant’s circus, Giraffe’s towers), following keys and routes (Penguin’s ice path, Unicorn’s rainbow route, Bunny’s path detective — plus one fully traceable acorn maze), and combining two clues (Owl’s secret code, Raccoon’s clue hunt and secret object, Dragon’s treasure, Panda’s balloons) — up to the Logic Castle graduation that mixes them all.

Ask “how did you know?” after every solve — explaining a rule out loud is the highest level of this whole class.

PLAY · SPOT THE DIFFERENCE

Fox’s Spot the Difference

Fox and Rabbit are having a picnic in both pictures, but five things are different! Look closely and circle each difference on Picture 2.

Drawing on the picture needs JavaScript. Everything else on this page works without it — and the matching worksheet brings this adventure to paper.

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

Spot-the-difference trains visual discrimination — the same eye-for-detail that later tells b from d on a page. Let your child point before tapping, and compare pictures aloud together: “In this one the hat is…?”

Illustration note: The printed art asks for 5 differences and truly contains exactly 5: the cap is blue then red, the butterfly yellow then pink, Rabbit holds a carrot then a flower, the apple is red then green, and one mushroom spot turns pink. The pink spot is the sneakiest — celebrate it loudest.

Prefer paper? The Fox’s Spot the Difference worksheet prints the same puzzle with room to draw, sort and circle — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.

PLAY · MAZE TRACING

Squirrel’s Acorn Maze

Help Squirrel find the golden acorn! Draw a line through the maze — and stay on the path.

Drawing on the picture needs JavaScript. Everything else on this page works without it — and the matching worksheet brings this adventure to paper.

Why this adventure helps.

Maze tracing builds planning and pencil control in one. Fingers work best to start; a stylus is a lovely bridge toward pencil-and-paper mazes. Hitting a wall just stops the line — no penalty, redraw any time.

PLAY · TWO-CLUE LOGIC

Fox’s Logic Picnic

Fox packed three picnics! Each clue shows a puzzle piece and a food. The piece’s colour matches the basket, and the food tells you what’s inside. Circle the basket that fits both clues!

Drawing on the picture needs JavaScript. Everything else on this page works without it — and the matching worksheet brings this adventure to paper.

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

This is early deductive reasoning: neither clue alone picks the basket, and saying it aloud — “green… and an apple… so the green apple basket!” — is the skill. The game mixes the baskets so the answer never sits in the same spot.

Illustration note: The real logic is two clues at once: the puzzle piece gives the basket colour and the food gives the contents. Each row always offers one right-colour-wrong-food and one right-food-wrong-colour basket, so both clues are needed.

Prefer paper? The Fox’s Logic Picnic worksheet prints the same puzzle with room to draw, sort and circle — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.

PLAY · SHAPE AND SIZE MATCHING

Fox’s Gear Workshop

Welcome to Fox’s workshop! Look at each machine’s empty spot, then circle the gear that fits.

Drawing on the picture needs JavaScript. Everything else on this page works without it — and the matching worksheet brings this adventure to paper.

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

Fitting pieces into machines rehearses shape-and-size reasoning. Say the WHY together: “the spot is round, so…”, “the spot is big, so…” — the explanation is the learning, and the game mixes the pieces every round.

Illustration note: Machine 1’s spot is round, so the round gear fits and the triangle and star cannot spin there. Machine 2’s spot is gear-shaped and big — the big green gear fits, the tiny purple gear is too small and a square cannot spin. Machine 3 is missing one gear colour: its empty spot is blue, so the blue gear completes the pair.

Prefer paper? The Fox’s Gear Workshop worksheet prints the same puzzle with room to draw, sort and circle — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.
